openingProblem.problem: Willy Brandt knelt in Warsaw in 1970. Ronald Reagan called the Soviet Union an 'evil empire' in 1983. Mikhail Gorbachev let Eastern Europe go in 1989. How much can a single leader change a global conflict?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: which of the three leaders mattered most, and why?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Willy Brandt and Ostpolitik, 1969–1974
chunks.body:
**Willy Brandt** shows that a leader who was not a superpower head of state could still change the Cold War. When his Social Democrats came to power in West Germany in 1969, Bonn's policy towards the East was frozen. Under Adenauer, West Germany had refused to recognise East Germany (the GDR) or any state that did, except the USSR, and had insisted that the division of Germany must be settled before any détente.

Brandt concluded that this policy had failed. America's refusal to contest the building of the Berlin Wall in 1961 had shown that the US would not risk war over the city, and his own experience as Mayor of West Berlin shaped his conclusions; in 1966 President Johnson made clear that American policy would not be held hostage to German reunification. The West's passive acceptance of the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 confirmed the lesson: if West Germans wanted to ease the division of Europe, they would have to deal with the East themselves. With his adviser Egon Bahr he devised **Ostpolitik**, based on "change through rapprochement": many small contacts that would gradually "overcome Yalta". Brandt dropped the claim that the GDR was illegitimate: there would be "one German nation, two German states".

The results came quickly. In 1970 West Germany signed treaties with Moscow and Warsaw accepting the post-war frontiers. In 1971 the four occupying powers agreed on Berlin, Moscow promising to make no unilateral changes and to ease movement. A Basic Treaty with the GDR was ratified in 1973, a treaty with Prague followed, and in 1974 the two German states exchanged permanent representatives. Brandt knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

Brandt's impact went beyond Germany. Judt argues that between the treaties with West Germany and the Helsinki Accords of 1975, which gave "retrospective confirmation and acceptance of Potsdam", the Soviet Union had achieved its objectives in Europe. Ostpolitik thus helped prepare the ground for the European security conference that NATO accepted in 1971. Brandt was forced out by a spy scandal in 1974, but his successors Schmidt and Kohl never abandoned his policy.

This mattered because Brandt reduced Cold War tension in its most dangerous place, Central Europe, which meant that détente in Europe had its own momentum, independent of the superpowers.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Brandt replaced Adenauer's refusal with engagement.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Engagement accepted the division of Germany for the time being.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Ostpolitik produced treaties that eased tension in Central Europe.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It also gave the USSR what it wanted: recognition of the borders.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Ostpolitik prepared the ground for Helsinki and outlasted Brandt.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the aims and achievements of Brandt's Ostpolitik between 1969 and 1974.
Discuss the view that Brandt's Ostpolitik did more to reduce Cold War tension in Europe than any superpower agreement with reference to the period 1969 to 1975.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Brandt's main aim was to ease the human costs of division by dealing directly with the East.
useItInAnEssay.prove: He accepted 'one German nation, two German states', and between 1970 and 1974 signed treaties with Moscow, Warsaw and Prague and a Basic Treaty with the GDR.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the borders that had divided Europe since 1945 were accepted, so fears of West German revanchism in the East were eased.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Ostpolitik also gave the USSR the recognition it had long sought, which Judt sees as a Soviet gain confirmed at Helsinki.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Brandt therefore achieved his aim of easing tension, at the price of accepting the division for the time being.

chunks.title: Ronald Reagan: confrontation, 1981–1985
chunks.body:
**Ronald Reagan** became US President in January 1981 determined to restore American strength. He pursued a comprehensive modernisation of US nuclear and conventional forces and tried to roll back Communism in South America, Africa and South Asia. His language was deliberately harsh. He spoke of leaving "Marxism-Leninism on the ash-heap of history" and called the Soviet Union an "evil empire". In 1983 he announced the **Strategic Defense Initiative** (SDI, "Star Wars"), a missile defence programme that Soviet leaders found highly threatening. In 1985 US defence spending rose by 6 per cent, an unprecedented peacetime increase.

But Reagan's record in these years was not simply one of confrontation. He wrote to three Soviet leaders in turn, Brezhnev, Andropov and Chernenko, urging them to ease tensions and negotiate arms reductions, and he lifted Carter's grain embargo as a gesture of good faith. Judt argues that much of the belligerence was rhetoric for a domestic audience: the same president was offering to withdraw American intermediate-range missiles if the Soviets dismantled theirs. Inside his government, Defence Secretary Weinberger distrusted arms control while Secretary of State Shultz favoured it; Reagan shared Shultz's wish to put human rights at the centre of negotiations.

What effect did Reagan's confrontation have? Admirers argue that it raised the cost of the arms race beyond what the Soviet Union could pay. Judt accepts that the American build-up came to be seen as "the cunningly crafted lever that bankrupted and ultimately broke the Soviet system", but adds: "This, however, is not quite accurate." In the short run, he argues, Reagan's hard line, and SDI in particular, made the ageing Soviet leadership "even less disposed to compromise". The low point came in the autumn of 1983, when Soviet negotiators walked out of the arms talks in Geneva.

This mattered because Reagan's first term increased both the pressure on the Soviet Union and the danger of the Cold War, which meant that his influence depended on whether a Soviet leader emerged who would respond to pressure with reform rather than resistance.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Much of the rhetoric was for a domestic audience.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: No major agreement was reached before 1985.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Confrontation hardened the old Soviet leadership in the short run.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: It raised the long-term cost of the arms race for the USSR.

chunks.title: Mikhail Gorbachev: new thinking, 1985–1989
chunks.body:
**Mikhail Gorbachev** became leader of the Soviet Communist Party in March 1985. Within a month he had halted Soviet missile deployments and offered to negotiate, proposing that both superpowers halve their strategic arsenals. Over the next four years he transformed Soviet foreign policy.

Why? Judt stresses that Gorbachev's priorities were domestic. A calmer international environment would buy time and support for his reforms at home, **perestroika** (restructuring) and **glasnost** (openness). Advised by Aleksandr Yakovlev, he concluded that the USSR could gain more control over its foreign relations "by well-calculated concessions than by fruitless confrontation". In October 1986 he declared that "ideology" was not an appropriate basis for foreign policy, a remarkable statement for a Soviet leader. He saw himself above all as a European statesman, speaking of a "European home", and built good relations with Western European leaders: Margaret Thatcher famously regarded him as a man she "could do business" with.

His decisions changed the Cold War. He met Reagan at five summits. In December 1987 they signed the INF Treaty, eliminating an entire class of nuclear missiles; by accepting Reagan's "zero option", Judt argues, Moscow conceded that a nuclear war in Europe could not be won. Gorbachev withdrew the Red Army from Afghanistan, the "bleeding wound": the last troops left on 15 February 1989. Above all, he made clear that the Soviet Union had abandoned the **Brezhnev Doctrine**, the policy of using force to keep Communist regimes in power. When Eastern Europeans rose in 1989, no Soviet tanks came.

At home his reforms opened the system too: from 1986 he freed the dissident Andrei Sakharov, relaxed censorship and stopped the jamming of foreign radio, and in 1989 the Soviet Union held its first more or less free elections since 1918.

This mattered because Gorbachev chose not to defend the Soviet empire by force, which meant that the Cold War in Europe could end peacefully.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Seen from Washington his concessions looked like a Reagan victory.

argumentsThatWork.claim: He reversed the arms race and left Afghanistan.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Reagan's 'zero option' shaped the INF Treaty.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Abandoning the Brezhnev Doctrine let Eastern Europe go.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The revolutions were made by Eastern Europeans themselves.

chunks.title: Comparing the leaders: who changed the Cold War?
chunks.body:
The three leaders worked in different regions and at different times, but each changed the Cold War.

**Reagan and Gorbachev together.** From 1985 the two men built a working relationship. At Reykjavik in October 1986 they discussed abolishing all nuclear weapons; they did not agree, but laid the basis for the INF Treaty of December 1987. In May 1988, standing in Red Square, Reagan declared that his phrase "evil empire" belonged to "another era". Reagan himself had moved: he had kept within SALT II's limits until 1985 while pursuing a reduction treaty (START), and with Shultz he made human rights central to US-Soviet talks. Reagan's successor, President George Bush, met Gorbachev at Malta in December 1989, where the two sides "buried the Cold War at the bottom of the Mediterranean". Gorbachev then accepted the reunification of Germany within NATO.

**Who mattered most?** The Office of the Historian concludes that the Cold War ended "nearly entirely peacefully, and on U.S. terms", a verdict that favours Reagan. Judt gives more weight to Gorbachev: his choices were driven by domestic priorities, and "the US played a remarkably small part in the dramas of 1989, at least until after the fact". Reagan raised the pressure, but it took a Soviet leader willing to respond with reform rather than resistance.

**Brandt's place.** Brandt worked earlier and on a smaller stage, but his Ostpolitik eased tension in Central Europe a decade and a half before Gorbachev. Like Gorbachev, he thought of the Cold War as a European problem to be solved by contacts rather than confrontation. In 1983 he even stood against Reagan's policy, urging 300,000 people in Bonn to reject new NATO missiles. His policy of accepting borders in order to ease human contact helped create the Helsinki framework, whose human rights clauses later aided the dissidents of 1989.

**Comparing types of leadership.** Reagan and Gorbachev were superpower leaders whose decisions could change the military balance. Brandt was the leader of a front-line state who changed the political climate in Europe. Each shows a different way in which an individual can shape a global conflict.

This mattered because the end of the Cold War required both pressure and reform, which meant that the roles of the leaders were complementary rather than rival explanations.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Bush, not Reagan, was President when the Cold War ended.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Historians differ on whose role was decisive.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both leaders' roles were shaped by circumstances.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Brandt changed the European climate earlier.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: His policy accepted division rather than ending it.

decodeKey.judgement: Whether Gorbachev outweighed Reagan, economics and popular movements

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev was the decisive individual, because only he could choose not to defend the Soviet empire by force; but he acted under economic strain and Reagan's pressure, and Eastern Europeans made the revolutions themselves.

arguments.claim: Gorbachev's new thinking and concessions (named factor first).
Reagan's pressure and the zero option.
Judt on the US role in 1989.

modelPlan.counter: The Office of the Historian says the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms'.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Who decided whether the Cold War ended? Gorbachev, because only Moscow could let Eastern Europe go.

segments.text: Gorbachev was the main reason for the end of the Cold War, because only he could decide not to defend the Soviet empire by force.
He signed the INF Treaty in 1987, withdrew from Afghanistan by February 1989 and abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine, so no Soviet tanks stopped the revolutions of 1989.
This meant that the Cold War in Europe could end peacefully, since its central military guarantee had been withdrawn.
However, Reagan's 'zero option' shaped the INF Treaty, and the Office of the Historian argues the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms'.
Gorbachev was therefore the decisive individual, though he acted in circumstances others had helped create.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Brandt's Ostpolitik did more to reduce Cold War tension in Europe than any superpower agreement.” Discuss with reference to the period 1969 to 1975.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim: Ostpolitik did more than superpower agreements
decodeKey.judgement: Whether Brandt's treaties mattered more than SALT and Helsinki

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely valid for Central Europe: Brandt's treaties accepted the borders that had caused most tension and prepared the ground for Helsinki; but superpower agreements such as the Berlin accord and SALT were needed to secure them.

arguments.claim: Against: the four-power Berlin agreement depended on the superpowers.
Against: Ostpolitik needed US-Soviet détente as its setting.

modelPlan.counter: Brandt acted only because the US had shown it would not fight for German unity, so the superpowers set the limits.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Where was tension greatest? In Central Europe, where Brandt's treaties addressed it directly.

segments.text: Brandt's Ostpolitik did more than any superpower agreement to reduce tension in Central Europe.
Between 1970 and 1974 Bonn signed treaties with Moscow, Warsaw and Prague accepting the post-war frontiers and a Basic Treaty with the GDR.
This meant that the borders that had fuelled fears of German revanchism were accepted, so, as Judt argues, the USSR achieved its objectives and Helsinki became possible.
However, the four-power agreement on Berlin in 1971 needed the superpowers, and Brandt acted only because the US had shown it would not fight for German unity.
The claim is therefore valid for Central Europe, though Ostpolitik worked within limits set by the superpowers.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the impact of Reagan on the Cold War between 1981 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far his policies, rather than Soviet choices, changed the Cold War

modelPlan.thesis: Reagan's impact was significant but double-edged: his rearmament raised the cost of the Cold War and his later partnership with Gorbachev produced the INF Treaty, but his early hard line hardened Soviet attitudes, and Soviet choices proved decisive.
modelPlan.counter: Judt argues that it is 'not quite accurate' to say Reagan's build-up broke the USSR.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: By what criterion? Change in the relationship: the decisive change came after 1985, when Gorbachev responded.

segments.text: Reagan's impact on the Cold War was significant but depended on Gorbachev's response.
Reagan announced SDI in 1983 and raised defence spending by 6 per cent in 1985, yet in December 1987 he signed the INF Treaty with Gorbachev.
This meant that he raised the pressure on the Soviet Union and then accepted partnership when it was offered, so the arms race was reversed.
However, Judt argues his hard line made the old Soviet leaders 'even less disposed to compromise', and that it is 'not quite accurate' to say his build-up broke the USSR.
Reagan's impact was therefore real but secondary to Gorbachev's decisions.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of Reagan and Gorbachev on the Cold War between 1981 and 1991.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.judgement: Whose impact was greater, and how they differed

modelPlan.thesis: Both leaders moved from confrontation to partnership and together reversed the arms race, but Reagan's impact lay in raising the pressure, whereas Gorbachev's lay in choosing not to defend the Soviet empire, which made his role decisive.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both negotiated the INF Treaty.
Difference: only Gorbachev could let Eastern Europe go.

modelPlan.counter: The Office of the Historian's verdict that the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms' favours Reagan.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Gorbachev's abandonment of the Brezhnev Doctrine, which no American could have decided.

segments.text: Reagan and Gorbachev both changed the Cold War, but in different ways.
Both signed the INF Treaty in 1987, but Reagan had first raised defence spending and announced SDI, whereas Gorbachev halted Soviet deployments and offered concessions.
This meant that Reagan raised the cost of the Cold War, while Gorbachev decided to stop paying it, so their policies were complementary.
However, the Office of the Historian argues the Cold War ended 'on U.S. terms', which gives Reagan's pressure more weight.
The decisive difference was therefore Gorbachev's choice not to defend the Soviet empire, which Judt sees as more important than American pressure.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the aims and achievements of Brandt's Ostpolitik between 1969 and 1974.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which aim mattered most, and which achievement lasted

modelPlan.thesis: Brandt aimed to ease the human costs of division by dealing directly with the East, and he achieved treaties accepting the post-war borders; but the price was accepting division for the time being.

arguments.claim: Aim: ease fears of revanchism and human contacts.
Achievement: popularity, Nobel Prize and continuity.

modelPlan.counter: Judt sees the treaties as a Soviet gain, completing Moscow's objectives with Helsinki.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which achievement lasted? The policy itself: Schmidt and Kohl never deviated from it.

segments.text: Brandt's main aim was to ease the division of Europe by dealing directly with the East.
Bahr's 'change through rapprochement' led to treaties with Moscow and Warsaw in 1970, the Berlin agreement of 1971 and the Basic Treaty ratified in 1973.
This meant that West Germany accepted the post-war borders, so human contacts grew and fears of revanchism eased.
However, Judt argues these treaties, with Helsinki, gave the USSR what it had long sought.
Ostpolitik therefore achieved its aim of easing tension, at the price of accepting division for the time being.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the impact of Gorbachev's foreign policy on Eastern Europe between 1985 and 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: How his choices connected to the revolutions of 1989

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev's foreign policy removed the threat of Soviet intervention and legitimised calls for reform, which allowed the peoples of Eastern Europe to overthrow their regimes peacefully in 1989.

arguments.claim: New thinking: ideology no basis for policy.

modelPlan.counter: The revolutions were made by Eastern Europeans; Gorbachev permitted rather than caused them.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: How did his choices connect to 1989? By removing the Soviet guarantee that had crushed protest in 1953, 1956 and 1968.

segments.text: Gorbachev's foreign policy made the revolutions of 1989 possible by removing the threat of Soviet intervention.
He declared in 1986 that ideology was no basis for foreign policy, withdrew from Afghanistan by February 1989 and abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine.
This meant that Eastern European regimes could no longer rely on Soviet tanks, so when popular protest came, they fell.
However, the revolutions were made by Eastern Europeans themselves; Gorbachev permitted change rather than causing it.
Gorbachev's impact was therefore decisive as a permissive condition of 1989.
